subject: Lebende Fremdsprache
title: Loved to Death: A Radio Feature on Overtourism
kernfrage: What happens when a beautiful place becomes too popular — and can you catch the key facts, opinions and attitudes in a radio report that weighs up the different voices?

intro.content: In this lesson you will listen to parts of a radio programme about „overtourism“ — what happens when too many visitors come to a beautiful place. Your teacher will read each recording aloud twice. You will not understand every single word, and you do not need to. First listen for the general idea; then listen again for the specific details each task asks about. It almost always helps to read the questions BEFORE you listen.

sections.title: Tuning In: Getting the Facts
sections.throughline: Aufbau der rezeptiven Hörkompetenz vom Globalverstehen zum selektiven Detailverstehen: Die Schüler:innen entnehmen zunächst Hauptaussagen und Schlüsselzahlen, dann gezielt Einzelinformationen und schließlich die Standpunkte verschiedener Sprecher:innen. Das Thema Overtourism ist bewusst gewählt — mit Hallstatt hat es einen unmittelbaren österreichischen Anker.
talking_points: Unterschied global – selektiv – detailliert: Warum liest man die Fragen VOR dem Hören? (Erwartungshaltung steuert die Aufmerksamkeit.)
Zahlen und Eigennamen (‚eight hundred' vs. ‚ten thousand', Hallstatt, Venice, Barcelona) sind typische Hörfallen — vor dem zweiten Durchgang bewusst machen.
Wie unterscheidet man beim Hören eine Tatsachenbehauptung von einer Meinung? Diese Frage wird in Section 2 vertieft.
Landeskunde-Brücke: Kennen die Schüler:innen Hallstatt oder ähnliche überlaufene Orte aus eigener Erfahrung?
extensions: Die Schüler:innen recherchieren eine echte Maßnahme gegen Overtourism (Venedig-Eintritt, Hallstatt-Barrieren, Kreuzfahrt-Limits) und berichten kurz auf Englisch.
Ein authentischer englischsprachiger Radio- oder Podcast-Ausschnitt zum selben Thema als Erweiterungs-Hörtext (natürliches Sprechtempo).
Fachübergreifend mit Geographie/GWB: Was macht einen Ort zu einem ‚Hotspot', und welche wirtschaftlichen Abhängigkeiten entstehen?

blocks.prompt:
You are going to hear the opening of a radio programme called “The Long View”. Read the four questions below FIRST. Then listen — your teacher will read the recording aloud twice — and note down what you hear.

[Your teacher reads:]
“Good evening, and welcome to The Long View. Tonight: the places we are loving to death. Fifty years ago, foreign travel was a luxury. Today, cheap flights and social media have put almost every corner of the planet within reach — and some of the world's most beautiful places are struggling under the weight of their own fame. Take Hallstatt, the tiny lakeside village in Upper Austria. Fewer than eight hundred people live there. Yet on a busy summer's day, the mayor says, as many as ten thousand visitors arrive — many staying less than an hour, just long enough to take a photograph and move on. Venice now charges day-trippers a fee to enter on its busiest weekends. In Barcelona, residents have marched through the streets with a blunt message for tourists: go home. Tonight we ask a simple question with no simple answer — who does a place belong to?”

1. Which two developments have put travel within reach of far more people today?
2. How many people live in Hallstatt, and how many visitors can arrive on a busy summer's day?
3. What has the city of Venice introduced?
4. What have residents in Barcelona done, and what is their message?
blocks.answer_key: 1. Cheap flights and social media. 2. Fewer than 800 people live there; up to 10,000 visitors can arrive on a busy summer's day. 3. An entry fee for day-trippers on its busiest weekends. 4. They have marched / protested through the streets; their message is “(tourists) go home”.
watch_outs: Zahlen sind die klassische Hörfalle: ‚fewer than eight hundred' (Einwohner) darf nicht mit ‚ten thousand' (Besucher) verwechselt werden — langsam und deutlich vorlesen, die Zahlen leicht betonen.
‚Loving to death' und ‚under the weight of their own fame' sind Redewendungen (etwas durch Übermaß zerstören) — nicht wörtlich verstehen; ggf. nach dem ersten Durchgang kurz klären.
Ehrlichkeitshinweis für die Lehrkraft: Die genannten Zahlen sind Aussagen des (fiktiven) Radioberichts — gerundete, plausible Richtwerte für die Hörübung, keine geprüfte Statistik.

blocks.prompt:
Now you will hear an interview from the same programme. A reporter talks to Margit, who runs a small bakery in a honeypot village. Listen twice. Decide whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE, and write down the words from the recording that prove your answer.

[Your teacher reads:]
Reporter: “I'm on the main street with Margit, who has run a small bakery here for over thirty years. Margit, has tourism been good for business?”
Margit: “Good and bad. Twenty years ago we had customers all year round — neighbours, families, people who knew our names. Now most of our visitors buy nothing at all. They photograph the shop, sometimes they come in just to use the toilet, and then they leave. The rents have risen so much that three of my neighbours have had to move away. My own children can't afford to live in the village where they grew up.”
Reporter: “So you'd prefer fewer tourists?”
Margit: “I'd prefer DIFFERENT tourists. People who stay a night, who eat in the restaurant, who actually want to know the place — not ten thousand people rushing through in an afternoon.”

statements: Margit has run her bakery for less than ten years.
According to Margit, most visitors today buy nothing from her shop.
Rising rents have forced some of her neighbours to move away.
Margit wants tourism to stop completely.
Margit's children have decided to move abroad to find work.

blocks.answer_key: 1. FALSE — “for over thirty years”. 2. TRUE — “most of our visitors buy nothing at all”. 3. TRUE — “the rents have risen so much that three of my neighbours have had to move away”. 4. FALSE — she wants “DIFFERENT tourists”, not none: “people who stay a night, who eat in the restaurant”. 5. FALSE — the recording only says her children “can't afford to live in the village”; nothing is said about working abroad.
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Bei der Begründung zählt ein tatsächliches Zitat / eine klar wiedererkennbare Textstelle, keine Paraphrase. Statement 5 ist korrekt als FALSE zu werten, weil die Aussage über die Textinformation hinausgeht (Overinterpretation).
watch_outs: Statement 4 ist die zentrale Verstehensfalle: ‚fewer tourists' (Reporterfrage) vs. Margits ‚DIFFERENT tourists' — wer nur die Frage hört, wählt fälschlich TRUE.
Statement 5 prüft die Abgrenzung ‚im Text belegt' vs. ‚plausibel dazugedacht' — häufig als TRUE geraten. Explizit einfordern: nur was hörbar gesagt wurde, zählt.
‚can't afford' und ‚rents have risen' ggf. vorentlasten, falls der Grundwortschatz der Klasse begrenzt ist.

levels: All judgements correct and based on what was said
One or two judgements slip on the tricky items (4/5)
Several judgements guessed without textual basis
Precise words from the recording quoted for each item
Evidence given but sometimes paraphrased
Little or no evidence; answers asserted

blocks.prompt:
The programme now lets four people with very different stakes sum up their view in one sentence. Listen twice, then match each voice (1–4) to the opinion (A–E) that best fits it. One opinion is NOT needed.

[Your teacher reads:]
1. (a hotel owner) “Tourism pays for everything here — the school bus, the doctor, the shops. Without visitors, this village would simply die.”
2. (a young resident) “I grew up here, but I can't afford a flat here any more. The whole place has become a museum that I'm not allowed to live in.”
3. (a tour guide) “The problem isn't the NUMBER of people, it's how they behave. A little respect — keeping the noise down, not blocking doorways — would change everything.”
4. (a day visitor) “I've got one day and a long list of places to see. I feel a bit guilty, but honestly I'll probably never come back, so I just want the photo.”

right: A — The village could not survive financially without its visitors.
B — The real problem is not how many tourists come, but how they behave.
C — Local people are being priced out of their own home town.
D — Visitors should be forced to pay a much higher entry fee.
E — Time pressure makes a visitor treat the place as just a photo stop.

blocks.answer_key: 1–A, 2–C, 3–B, 4–E. Opinion D is the distractor — nobody in this clip calls for a higher entry fee (a fee was only mentioned earlier, about Venice).
watch_outs: D ist ein bewusster Distraktor: Weil im Intro (t1) eine Gebühr in Venedig vorkam, wählen manche D vorschnell. Darauf hinweisen, dass in DIESEM Ausschnitt niemand eine Gebühr fordert.
Voice 3 sagt ausdrücklich ‚isn't the NUMBER of people' — wer nur ‚people/number' hört, ordnet leicht falsch zu. Auf die Verneinung achten.
Sicherstellen, dass die vier Stimmen mit erkennbar unterschiedlicher Sprechhaltung vorgelesen werden — das ist die eigentliche Hörleistung.

sections.title: Reading Between the Lines
sections.throughline: Übergang vom Wörtlichen zum Impliziten: Die Schüler:innen erschließen Sprecherhaltung, unterscheiden Fakt und Meinung, folgen einer komplexeren Argumentation und geben schließlich das Gehörte adressatengerecht weiter (Sprachmittlung). Hier zeigt sich Oberstufen-Niveau: nicht nur WAS gesagt wurde, sondern WIE und WARUM.
talking_points: Welche sprachlichen Signale verraten eine Haltung? (Wortwahl, Ironie, Vergleiche, rhetorische Fragen wie ‚Honestly?').
Fakt vs. Meinung: An welchen Formulierungen erkennt man eine überprüfbare Aussage gegenüber einer Wertung?
Bei der Sprachmittlung (t6) geht es um AUSWAHL: Was ist für die adressierte Person wirklich relevant? Weglassen ist Teil der Leistung.
Wie bewertet man ein Argument fair, ohne die eigene Meinung als Maßstab zu setzen? (t5)
extensions: Debatte im Anschluss: ‚This class would put a strict daily limit on visitors to Hallstatt.' — die gehörten Argumente werden zu eigenen Redebeiträgen.
Die Schüler:innen schreiben Daniels Argument (t4) zu einem kurzen Leserbrief-Gegen- ODER Zustimmungstext um (Transfer Hören → Schreiben).
Vergleich zweier echter Schlagzeilen zum Thema (pro/contra) — dieselbe Tatsache, unterschiedliche Wertung: Medienkompetenz.

blocks.prompt:
Not everyone agrees that the answer is fewer visitors. Listen twice to Daniel Reisz, who runs bus tours to the region, and then answer the questions below in full sentences.

[Your teacher reads:]
Daniel: “Honestly? I think this whole ‚overtourism' panic is exaggerated. For eight months of the year these villages are half empty and desperate for customers. The crowding lasts a few weeks in summer. We don't close a motorway because it's busy on a Friday evening — we manage it. Spread the visitors across the year, book time slots, put the money from tickets back into the village, and the problem mostly disappears. What I hear from some campaigners sounds less like a real transport problem and more like they simply don't want to share their beautiful home.”

(a) What is Daniel's overall attitude towards the idea of “overtourism”? Quote two or three words that show it.
(b) Daniel makes a comparison to explain his point. What does he compare the busy villages to, and what is that comparison meant to suggest?
(c) Pick ONE thing Daniel says that is a fact and ONE that is his opinion. How can you tell the difference?
(d) Look at his final sentence. What is he suggesting about the real motives of some campaigners?
blocks.answer_key: (a) He thinks it is overstated / not a real crisis: “exaggerated”, “panic”. (b) He compares the villages to a motorway that is busy on a Friday evening: just as you manage a busy road instead of closing it, you should manage peak tourist times instead of cutting visitor numbers — the crowding is a manageable peak, not a reason to turn people away. (c) FACT (checkable): e.g. “for eight months of the year these villages are half empty” / “the crowding lasts a few weeks in summer”. OPINION (a judgement): e.g. “the panic is exaggerated” / campaigners “don't want to share their beautiful home”. A fact can in principle be measured or checked; an opinion expresses a personal evaluation. (d) He implies their concern is not really about crowd management at all but about selfishness — that they simply don't want to share the place with outsiders.
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Für (c) sind verschiedene Zuordnungen zulässig, solange die Begründung stimmt (überprüfbar vs. wertend). Für (d) zählt jede Antwort, die den unterstellten Vorwurf (Egoismus / ‚nicht teilen wollen') erkennt.
watch_outs: ‚analyze' heißt: über das Wörtliche hinausgehen. Manche Schüler:innen fassen Daniel nur zusammen, statt seine HALTUNG zu benennen — gezielt nach den wertenden Wörtern fragen.
Der Motorway-Vergleich (b) wird oft wörtlich genommen (‚er redet über Autobahnen'). Die übertragene Bedeutung (Spitzen managen statt sperren) einfordern.
Fakt/Meinung (c): ‚half empty for eight months' klingt für manche wie eine Meinung — klarmachen, dass es prinzipiell messbar und damit ein (behaupteter) Fakt ist.

levels: Attitude named precisely and supported with the right words
Attitude broadly correct but weakly evidenced
Only literal content restated; attitude not identified
Clear example of each with a correct, explained distinction
Correct examples but shaky explanation
Categories confused
Full, mostly accurate sentences; ideas clear
Understandable with errors that do not block meaning
Errors frequently obscure meaning

blocks.prompt:
Finally, the phone lines. Two callers, two very different views. Listen twice, then complete the task.

[Your teacher reads:]
Caller 1 (Priya): “I understand that people are frustrated, but tourism is not the enemy. It has lifted whole regions out of poverty. The answer is better management, not blaming visitors. If we turn people away, we lose the money that keeps these communities alive — and we send a message that some places are only for the rich who can afford to stay a week.”
Caller 2 (Tomás): “With respect, that's the argument we've heard for twenty years, and the situation has only got worse. At some point ‚better management' becomes an excuse for doing nothing. When local families are driven out and the streets are impassable, the town has already lost the thing that made it special. Sometimes the only real solution is a hard limit on numbers, even if it costs money.”

(a) Sum up each caller's main position in ONE sentence of your own.
(b) Whose argument do you personally find more convincing, and why? You must refer to at least one specific point that EACH caller made.
blocks.answer_key: (a) Priya: tourism brings prosperity and should be managed better, not cut — turning visitors away would harm communities and make places elitist. Tomás: “better management” has failed for twenty years and become an excuse; once residents are pushed out the town has already lost its character, so sometimes a hard cap on numbers is the only real solution. (b) Open. A strong answer states a clear preference AND engages with a specific point from each caller (e.g. agreeing with Priya's ‚only for the rich' worry, but conceding Tomás's point that twenty years of ‚management' have not worked). Reward genuine weighing of both sides over a one-sided opinion.
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Beide Positionen sind vertretbar; bewertet wird die Qualität der Abwägung und der konkrete Bezug auf JE einen Punkt beider Anrufer:innen, nicht die gewählte Seite.
watch_outs: Häufigster Fehler bei (b): eigene Meinung ohne Rückbezug auf das Gehörte (‚I think too many tourists is bad'). Auf den geforderten Bezug zu JE einem konkreten Punkt bestehen.
Bei (a) neigen Schüler:innen dazu, wörtlich mitzuschreiben statt in EINEM eigenen Satz zusammenzufassen — Paraphrase einfordern.
Tomás' ‚that's the argument we've heard for twenty years' ist ironisch-kritisch gemeint — die abtuende Haltung sollte erkannt werden, nicht als neutrale Info.

levels: Both positions summed up accurately in the student's own words
One position clear, the other vague or partly wrong
Positions confused or merged
Clear stance that engages with a specific point from EACH caller
Stance stated but only one caller's point used
Opinion asserted with no reference to what was heard
Ideas connected with a good range of language; errors minor
Adequate range; some errors but meaning stays clear
Limited range; errors impede meaning

blocks.prompt:
Your exchange partner from England had to leave the room and missed most of the programme. In English, write them a short message (about 80–100 words) that tells them:
- what the programme was about
- the example of Hallstatt (with one or two key facts)
- the TWO main sides of the argument you heard.

Choose only the information your partner really needs — you cannot include everything, so leave out the small details and keep the message clear and useful.
blocks.answer_key: Model message (approx. 95 words): “Hi! You missed a good radio programme about ‚overtourism' — when too many tourists overwhelm a beautiful place. The main example was Hallstatt in Austria: fewer than 800 people live there, but up to 10,000 visitors can come on one summer day, and locals are being priced out. There were two sides. Some people want to limit or change visitor numbers to protect residents. Others say tourism keeps these villages alive and the real answer is better management — spreading visitors out, not turning them away. The big question was: who does a place belong to?” Accept any coherent 80–100-word briefing that selects the key facts and both positions and leaves out minor detail.
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Es handelt sich um Sprachmittlung: Bewertet werden die AUSWAHL relevanter Informationen, die Adressatenorientierung (verständlich für die Partnerin/den Partner) und sprachliche Klarheit — NICHT Vollständigkeit. Wer alle Details übernimmt, hat die Aufgabe (‚choose only what your partner needs') verfehlt.
watch_outs: Sprachmittlung ist NICHT Übersetzung und nicht ‚alles wiedergeben': Wer den gesamten Hörtext nacherzählt, verfehlt das Auswahlkriterium. Weglassen ist Teil der Leistung.
Beide Seiten des Arguments müssen vorkommen — viele geben nur EINE Position wieder. Explizit einfordern.
Wortzahl (80–100) im Blick behalten: zu kurz → Kerninfos fehlen; zu lang → Auswahl misslungen. Register darf informell sein (Nachricht an eine:n Freund:in).

levels: Only the key facts and both sides included; minor detail rightly left out
Mostly relevant but some clutter or a missing key point
Poor selection: overloaded with detail or key points missing
Both positions communicated clearly and fairly
Both present but one is unclear
Only one side conveyed
Clear, well-organised message suited to the reader; word count met
Understandable; small issues with flow or length
Hard to follow or badly off the word count
Mostly accurate; errors do not affect meaning
Errors present but meaning clear
Frequent errors that impede meaning
